implementation_state: The upstream contracts this node was blocked on are now closed: ACCOUNT, NEWAPI, I2, I3 and I4 all pass their gates, so the blocked_by set is emptied and the node is no longer waiting on upstream. One of its three own gates has moved further than the previous revision of this record said. Backend lifecycle ownership: the account reconciler is not only called from core, it now has a desktop command behind the account feature, and Snapshot carries an account_available flag so a dashboard can ask whether this build has the subsystem at all rather than discovering the absence from a failed call — that flag is separate from account_maintenance_available because the two answer different questions and account-maint implies account. The check-in runtime goes further and owns a headed browser session per (provider, account): a WAF challenge holds that session rather than destroying it, so a resume continues the same session and never asks the operator to authenticate twice, and a minute timer walks the declared accounts and starts the ones a pure decision function calls due, with the settlement history durable across restarts. Real surfaces: four Tauri commands and a per-account maintenance row with start, resume, cancel and a written record of what was observed rather than what was hoped for, and the row renders the six scheduler answers separately on purpose, because "nothing happened" would send an operator to change a setting that is not the problem — one of them is the user's own choice, one is a gap in their declaration, and only two mean a schedule is quietly counting down. THE CLAUSE THAT NAMED THREE ENGINES WITH NO CALLER WAS HALF STALE AND IS NOW ENTIRELY SO, and the direction of the error is the useful part. TakeoverStore stopped being a fixture when the takeover commands and page landed, and this record was simply never re-read; that is the same failure E-143 records for three clauses in UI's only note, where a sentence written before the surface existed outlived the surface. MigrationExecutor and the rollback path were accurate, and they are now wired: four commands registered ungated in lib.rs, because zroutery_core::migration is compiled into every build and unlike account or ml there is no configuration in which they are absent. The Cutover page builds a typed plan from real detected state, confirms it against a fingerprint, captures the client config byte for byte before anything is written, and renders the result with rolled_back and state as two separate claims. The product confirmation and rollback UI is no longer merely conceptual, and the distinction this record drew holds in the code: the check-in confirmation interrupts a human and resumes, the cutover confirmation guards a write that can be undone, and the rollback is offered exactly where the state machine permits it -- Failed, and nowhere else, because rollback_with ignores a refused transition and would restore the bytes while the record denied it. The rollback semantics question this record listed as open has been settled the only way it could be, by rendering rather than by deciding: a rollback that restored nothing reports rolled_back false and the panel says so, while the machine still says RolledBack, and both are shown because each is true and the other does not imply it. The core has the pieces a surface would need — durable ownership with compare-and-swap, conflict resolution applied on release, accurate rollback reporting, and an account reconciler that publishes outcomes rather than only successes. What is unexercised is named rather than gestural: the check-in row is the one surface here that a person has driven in the running application, and doing so found three browser-lifecycle defects no mock could have, fixed with tests that fail by name when inverted; the scheduler against a real relay console, an interval elapsing against a live panel and any WAF challenge are still asserted against fixtures only. See E-120, E-122, E-131, E-132, E-134, E-135.
unblock_condition: Close the Account, NewAPI, I2, I3, and I4 lifecycle contracts before adding user-facing controls.
notes: No placeholder control is treated as a product lifecycle.

No longer blocked on upstream: ACCOUNT, NEWAPI, I2, I3, and I4 all pass their gates and their blocked_by sets are empty. The status is PARTIAL because its own three gates are unmet, not because it is waiting on another node.

The check-in row is the one surface here that has been driven by a real browser, and its check-in control has been shown to receive a trusted event. It has now been exercised by a person in the running application, and doing so found three browser-lifecycle defects that no unit test and no mock could have: a finished attempt never closed its browser, a cancel arriving mid-attempt freed the account while a browser was still holding its profile directory, and shutdown reported success while the browser survived. Two Chrome processes on one user-data-dir is what Chrome answers by damaging the profile, which is the dialog the operator saw. All three are fixed with tests that fail by name when the fix is inverted. What is still unexercised: the scheduler against a real relay console, an interval elapsing against a live panel, and any WAF challenge, so everything asserted about those is asserted against fixtures.

Migration and takeover now both have commands and pages, so the sentence above that listed them among the engines with no caller has been corrected in place rather than dropped, keeping what is still true about the scheduler and the browser session.

The Cutover page deliberately does NOT offer a second way to put a client on the gateway. Takeover is the better tool for that and for taking it off again; a cutover exists for the case takeover cannot answer, which is a run that failed or was interrupted and whether the file came back. Two surfaces for one job would have been surface area without a capability, which is the mistake this node's own first note warns against.

What remains unexercised is one path and it is named: a cutover that reaches Completed needs a live gateway answering /health, so a person has not yet driven one end to end in the running application, and every claim about that path rests on fixtures.

MOVED TO DONE, AND THE LAST THING THAT HELD IT WAS A PROOF RATHER THAN A FEATURE. The node was PARTIAL with one thing left that no gate could decide: the `Completed` state of a cutover had been asserted only by fixtures that never put the steps together, so the state machine's happy path was unproven even though every one of its steps was proven on its own. It is proven now, and the way it was proven is the way the project has wanted things proven all along: a real `axum` server on an ephemeral port answering exactly what the gateway's `/health` answers, a real file in a real temporary directory, a real snapshot taken before the run, and the whole sequence — then the undo, which puts the original bytes back. The gate that drives it lives in `crates/zroutery-core/tests/migration_completion_test.rs`, and the desktop's own test pins the plan that gate drives, so the engine's proof and the product's plan cannot drift apart. Both were driven to failing first: a drifted body mark and a reordered plan each fail by name.

TWO THINGS THE WORK FOUND, BOTH OF WHICH WERE DOCUMENTS OVERCLAIMING. The plan's port step was documented as a pre-flight guard — "the port must be free, checked before anything is written" — and it is not one: `StartZroutery` reports a port that is in use and carries on. The behaviour is right and the document was wrong. The port a cutover switches to is usually Zroutery's own, and Zroutery is usually already running there, so a port in use is the ordinary case rather than a collision; what decides whether the holder is the right service is the endpoint check and its body marker, and a port number cannot tell them apart. So the action now says what it does, the plan says what it does, and the gate says so too: a taken port is reported, not fatal, and the check that decides is the last step. The second was the same shape: the plan's own comment claimed the port check was "checked before anything is written rather than discovered when the endpoint does not answer", and the file is in fact written before the endpoint is asked. The snapshot is what makes that safe, and the gate now proves the undo.

WHAT IS STILL TRUE, AND IS NOT A REASON TO HOLD THE NODE. The cutover page has not been driven by a person in the running application; the check-in row remains the one surface here that has been, and driving it is what found the three browser-lifecycle defects E-120 records. The scheduler against a real relay console, an interval elapsing against a live panel and any WAF challenge are still asserted against fixtures only. The `NEWAPI` node keeps its own two reasons, which this node does not own and does not move: the integration has never met a real panel, and the subsystem is still only reachable under an opt-in feature.
